forecasts.label: Capital financing requirement
forecasts.note: Restated at each quarterly return. The Q4 restatement comes from the annual return itself, so it lands on the outturn by construction — the interesting movement is Q1 to Q3.

forecasts.label: Interest payable
forecasts.note: The council's own full-year forecast, restated at each quarterly return.

forecasts.label: Revenue spending (net current expenditure)
forecasts.note: The full-year forecast of net current expenditure — the running cost of services — restated each quarter against the same measure at outturn.

forecasts.label: Capital expenditure
forecasts.note: Total capital spending forecast each quarter (the capital payments return) against the annual capital outturn. Capital spending not met from grants or receipts is what turns into new borrowing, so a forecast running ahead of outturn is a borrowing signal.

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter
in_year.note: Per quarter, not cumulative. The quarterly return is a lighter collection than the annual one and sums to roughly 92% of it nationally, so the two are shown apart rather than added together.

news_drafts.headline: Mid Suffolk's £4m of LOBO loans left unchanged in 2025/26 as lender did not use rate option
news_drafts.lead:
Mid Suffolk Council's £4m of LOBO loans were left unchanged through 2025/26. A LOBO is a bank loan where, on set dates, the lender may propose a higher interest rate and the council may then repay the loan in full instead of accepting it. The lender, Dexia Credit Local, did not use that option, according to the council's annual treasury management report for 2025-26 (treasury management is how a council borrows, invests its spare cash and manages the risks of both). "The lender has not exercised its option during 2025/26," the report says. It was before the meeting on 24 September 2026.

Dexia can propose a rate increase on 22 February and 22 August each year. If it does, the council can accept the new rate or repay the loan at par, meaning the sum originally borrowed. The report gives the average rate on the loans as 4.21%.

Had a higher rate been proposed and refused, the council would have had to replace the £4m with new borrowing, a step known as refinancing. Over the same year, rates on loans from the Public Works Loan Board, the government's lending arm for councils and the source of most council borrowing, rose by 34 basis points (0.34 percentage points). The two call dates come round again each year while the loans remain.

news_drafts.headline: Babergh and Mid Suffolk face £4.9m loan loss as housing ventures falter
news_drafts.lead: Babergh and Mid Suffolk councils are writing off nearly £5m on failed housing and commercial property ventures, with external auditors flagging concerns about their financial controls. Babergh Growth Ltd's housing scheme at a former council office is expected to lose £4.889m—an increase from £3.1m in one year—because units are not selling. Mid Suffolk scrapped a second housing development, writing off £877k in costs, though the land later sold for £2.7m. Both councils have also recognised £434k expected credit loss each on £43.3m loans to CIFCO Ltd, a commercial property investment company that is deferring interest payments. The councils are additionally struggling to deliver infrastructure projects: Mid Suffolk has £12m in unspent Community Infrastructure Levy funds allocated since 2018/19, with walking and cycling projects achieving just 0.7% spend despite allocating £3.3m to 13 schemes. External auditors have recommended the Statement of Accounts process be subject to ongoing monitoring.

findings.paper_title: MC/26/14 CIFCO Business Plan Review Council Report
findings.headline: Portfolio energy efficiency substantially improved to 57.5% at EPC C or above, targeting 75.9%
findings.detail: CIFCO's energy performance certificates have improved significantly, with 57.5% of properties now rated C or above, compared to 41.8% in 2022. The portfolio now includes one A+ rated property and has no F or G rated properties. Planned capital works over the next two years are projected to reach 75.9% at C or above.
findings.matters: Better EPC ratings reduce future regulatory compliance risk, support higher rental rates, improve asset quality and future-proof the portfolio against tightening energy efficiency regulations.
findings.figures: 57.5% at EPC C or above in 2025/26 vs 41.8% in 2022, planned to reach 75.9%
findings.quote: 57.5% of the CIFCO portfolio now has an EPC rating of C or above and CIFCO are pleased that it now also owns an A+ rated property and does not have any properties within band F and G... This has shown a significant improvement from 2022, from 41.8% to 57.5%... Further planned works during the next two financial years are estimated to result in 75.9% of the portfolio being rated C and above.

findings.paper_title: MC/26/14 CIFCO Business Plan Review Council Report
findings.headline: Asset disposal strategy underway, with Omron House sale completed and further disposals planned for 2026/27
findings.detail: CIFCO is executing its strategy to reduce large single-let office properties and rebalance portfolio weighting from office to industrial sectors. One disposal (Omron House) occurred in 2025/26 with a further disposal planned for early 2026/27. Sale proceeds fund energy improvements and refurbishments to increase income and repay debt interest. Success of this strategy is critical to managing void risk.
findings.matters: The councils' ability to improve returns and manage void risk depends on executing this sales strategy. If property market conditions deteriorate, planned sales may not materialise and the councils may be unable to fund improvements or service debt as projected.
findings.figures: one disposal in 2025/26 (Omron House), further disposal planned early 2026/27
findings.quote: During the 2025/26 period, this strategy has started to be implemented, seeing the sale of Omron House to reduce void risk. In the medium term, this will reduce the funds weighting in the office sector and likely to increase the industrial sector weighting. Capital raised from sales will fund energy improvement works and refurbishments to increase income and where appropriate may be used to repay debt interest.

findings.paper_title: MC/26/14 CIFCO Business Plan Review Council Report
findings.headline: Portfolio value under pressure from voids and lease expiries, particularly in office sector
findings.detail: While the portfolio stabilised with a 0.25% like-for-like increase, more than half the properties saw value growth or remained stable. However, properties facing lease expiries or voids—particularly in the office sector—have experienced value reductions. This concentration of risk in office holdings remains the focus of management attention.
findings.matters: Asset valuations underpin the councils' equity investment value and collateral for the debt. Continued devaluation in office properties erodes security and equity cushion.
findings.figures: 0.25% overall increase on like-for-like basis (£200k), but losses concentrated in void and lease-expiry properties, particularly office sector
findings.quote: The portfolio value has stabilised this year with a small increase of 0.25% overall (£200k) on a like for like basis... More than half of the properties have seen value growth or remained stable. The remaining properties have seen a reduction - the most impacted are those properties with impending lease expiries or voids, particularly those in the office sector.

findings.paper_title: MC/26/14 CIFCO Business Plan Review Council Report
findings.headline: Councils' borrowing costs consume 60% of CIFCO's contracted rents, leaving narrow margin for adverse moves
findings.detail: The councils' interest costs in servicing their CIFCO loans equal 60% of the rental income CIFCO receives. This generated a net return of £1.026m (0.80-1.27% on capital deployed) in 2025/26, with interest income currently exceeding interest costs. However, this narrow margin creates significant vulnerability to rental shortfalls or interest rate increases.
findings.matters: A lender would see £49.58m of borrowed capital generating only 0.80-1.27% net return with minimal headroom. A small adverse move in rents or rates could flip the investment cash-flow negative.
findings.figures: interest costs equivalent to approximately 60% of contracted rent, net return of 0.80% (Babergh) and 1.27% (Mid Suffolk)
findings.quote: The Councils' total interest repayments in respect of loans taken out to fund CIFCO equated to £3, 363m in 202 5/26 which is equivalent to an average of approximately 60% of the current contracted rent payable to CIFCO (3 2% Babergh DC & 28% Mid Suffolk DC). Income from CIFCO exceeds the Councils' cost of debt delivering a net income. Net income in 202 5/26 was £ 1.026m (Babergh £0.399m and Mid Suffolk £0. 627m)

findings.paper_title: MC/26/14 CIFCO Business Plan Review Council Report
findings.headline: CIFCO using deferment facility with £1.3m outstanding and £486k per annum additional deferments planned
findings.detail: CIFCO has drawn on a 10% deferment facility to manage cashflow and capital works. Outstanding deferments amount to £1.318m plus £71.8k interest as of March 2026. The business plan proposes additional deferments of £973k (£486k per annum), effectively pushing repayment further into the future and indicating cash flow pressures.
findings.matters: Deferments increase total debt obligations and indicate the company is struggling to meet scheduled repayments from operational cash flow. Repayment depends on asset sales proceeds succeeding as planned.
findings.figures: £1,318,757 in prior deferments with £71,838 interest, £973,596 additional deferments proposed (£486k per annum)
findings.quote: The balance from previous deferments is £1,318,757 with additional interest of £71,838 up to 31 March 2026. The proposed deferments over the business plan period equate to a total of £973,596 (£486k per annum). Deferments will only be drawn down if required and will be repaid through sales income or an annual payment plan.
